summary:
Schleswig-Holstein stands under the German national framework. Legal gender recognition runs through the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force since 1 November 2024, and under its mechanics a prisoner's placement follows the legal gender entry unless state law provides an exclusion. Schleswig-Holstein has no statute of its own governing the placement of trans prisoners, so the SBGG rules and the July 2026 placement case are the operative provisions for a visitor who is detained here.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate a statutory binary men-and-women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been applied only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 raises constitutional doubts about trans-targeted exception clauses in state law.

How the exception is applied remains unsettled. A report of 16 July 2026 covers a German court sending a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement, whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, to a men's prison amid public outcry over women's-prison safety; the case drove the state-level prison-placement law debate. DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities; that is a single-city provision, and no equivalent Schleswig-Holstein corrections guidance is on file.

Screening is a documented flashpoint. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued that month restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

The national conversion-therapy ban approved on 7 May 2020 applies in Schleswig-Holstein as elsewhere. No Schleswig-Holstein statute or ordinance specific to trans people is in force.
tangentialFactors:
The direction of travel across the German states is uneven and contested. Schleswig-Holstein has no trans-specific statute or ordinance in force, while other states have moved to legislate: Rhineland-Palatinate's prison act gained a § 17 on trans placement on 1 March 2026, and the Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 questions whether exception clauses of that kind survive constitutional review. A visitor held in custody therefore faces a national default rule rather than a local one.

The July 2026 placement case became the reference point for the state-level debate, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility and critics calling the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. Placement was to be reviewed at intake in the earlier handling of the same matter in August 2025.

On official posture toward conversion therapy, Schleswig-Holstein was one of five states, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Saarland, to table a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019 and reported by Zeit Online on 10 April 2019. The Bundestag approved the federal ban on 7 May 2020.

Facility-access disputes in neighbouring states are a proxy for what a visitor may encounter: the sauna guideline and the Berlin venue reporting show that women-protected spaces are handled venue by venue rather than by a single rule.
localsOnly:
Residents of Schleswig-Holstein have no state-level trans statute to rely on; gender recognition, prison placement and anti-discrimination claims run through federal law, principally the Self-Determination Act and the Equal Treatment Act.

People held in custody in the state are placed under the SBGG rule that placement follows the legal gender entry unless state law excludes it, with no Schleswig-Holstein exclusion on the books. Whether corrections authorities here apply that rule in practice is not documented in the sources.

The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, is the resident-facing support route: a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance with an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base addressing underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

Residents who are victims of hostile incidents can use those reporting channels, and the constitutional question raised on 18 March 2026 about trans-targeted exception clauses in state prison law bears directly on anyone challenging a placement decision.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Schleswig-Holstein-specific enforcement series, border or document practice, event-security finding, or corrections-authority guidance on trans detainees is on file; the sources describe the national position and, for illustration, other states and cities.

Whether Schleswig-Holstein prisons in fact apply the SBGG placement rule, and how intake review is conducted here, is unresolved in the sources.

The outcome of BASHKKA's June 2025 Equal Treatment Act complaint over the 23 November 2024 Frankfurt Airport screening is unresolved; the sources establish the filing and her account, not a decision.

Application of the January 2025 Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline to venues in Schleswig-Holstein is not sourced; the venue-level reporting cited concerns Berlin.

The reach of the Berlin prison service's trans, inter and non-binary information page beyond that city's facilities is not established.
